blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: This tree follows the topics and the problem list of NeetCode's roadmap (the NeetCode 150), with a learning page written for this site for each topic. The explanations and Java templates are ours; the problems belong to LeetCode, and each one links to its LeetCode page.

Instead of two nested loops that try every pair, keep **two indices** and move them according to a rule, so that each index only travels once through the data. The work drops from O(n²) to O(n).

There are two shapes:

- **Opposite ends.** One pointer at the start, one at the end, moving towards each other. It works when the data is **sorted** (or has a monotone property) so that moving a pointer in a direction has a predictable effect: Two Sum II, 3Sum, Container With Most Water, palindrome checks.
- **Same direction (fast and slow).** Both pointers start at the left; one reads ahead while the other marks where to write. It is used to compact or partition an array in place, and to detect cycles in linked lists.
"sorted array", "pair or triplet that sums to", "in place", "without extra space", "palindrome", "remove duplicates".
blocks.title: Signal words

blocks.text: The reasoning behind opposite-end pointers is a **discard argument**: when the sum is too small, the smaller element can never be part of *any* valid pair with the remaining elements, so you drop it safely. Being able to say that sentence is what interviewers listen for.

blocks.title: TwoPointers.java

blocks.text: **What to notice.** In `threeSum`, sorting costs O(n log n) and the double loop O(n²), so the total is O(n²): the best known for the problem. In `trap`, only the side with the *lower* wall is processed, because that side's water level is already decided by its own maximum.

- **Unsorted input.** Opposite-end pointers need order. If the array is unsorted and you must return indices (Two Sum), use a hash map instead, because sorting loses the original positions.
- **Duplicates in 3Sum.** Skip repeated values for *every* position, or the same triplet appears many times.
- **`l < r` versus `l <= r`.** Use `<` when the two pointers must be different elements.
- **Off-by-one on the inner `while`s** that skip characters: always re-check `l < r`.

The area is limited by the shorter wall times the distance. Moving the taller wall inward can only reduce the distance and cannot raise the limiting height, so it can never beat the current area. Moving the shorter wall is the only move that might improve it, so you may discard the shorter wall for good.
blocks.title: Interview angle: How do you justify moving the shorter wall in Container With Most Water?
Key points
blocks.text:
- Two pointers turn O(n²) pair searches into one O(n) pass
- Opposite ends need sorted data or a monotone property; same direction compacts or partitions in place
- Justify each move with a discard argument
- Sort and skip duplicates for 3Sum
- Use a hash map, not pointers, when you need original indices from unsorted data

items.question: Why does Two Sum II work with two pointers but plain Two Sum does not?
items.answer: Two Sum II gives a sorted array, so a sum that is too small means the left element is too small for every remaining partner and a too-large sum means the right one is too big. Plain Two Sum is unsorted, and sorting would lose the indices, so a hash map is the right tool.

items.question: What is the time and space complexity of 3Sum with sorting and two pointers?
items.answer: O(n²) time (sorting O(n log n) plus n iterations of an O(n) scan) and O(1) extra space apart from the output and sorting.

items.question: What does the slow pointer represent when removing duplicates in place?
items.answer: The next position to write: everything before it is the compacted result, and the fast pointer reads ahead looking for the next different value.
